building jarvis in your pocket This is exactly how I did it, no gatekeeping. I wanted a way to talk to my local Hermes agent quickly and easily. I’ll share my entire local AI setup with Hermes and my Second Brain soon, but in short my Hermes agent bounces between Qwen 3.8 27b for easy stuff, and GPT OSS 120b for more complex tasks. But realistically you can do this with any model that’s capable of handling simple queries. I purchased an M5Stack Stopwatch which is essentially a tiny computer built on the ESP32-S3 chip. It already has Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and a motion sensor in it, all packed into a round AMOLED stopwatch. All it needs, is a firmware. When I was originally trying to get one of these, they were all coming directly from China, which would take weeks. Fortunately I found that DigiKey had stock of them and I was able to get my hands on it much quicker. From there, I gave Claude Code the following prompt to build the firmware and Hermes plugin: “Build a Hermes plugin and ESP32 firmware so I can chat with my Hermes agent from a little pet on my esp32’s screen over local Wi-Fi. Keep it simple and walk me through it.” But this only worked if you and your device were on the same local Wi-Fi network. So I built in a redundant direct Bluetooth connection using this prompt: “Add Bluetooth as a backup. If the pet can’t reach Hermes over Wi-Fi, have it switch to Bluetooth LE with my PC automatically, and switch back to Wi-Fi when it’s available again.” Then finally, I wanted to be able to access it from anywhere so I built in a Tailscale option that I can flip on whenever I’m away from my Hermes computer (like the personal AI server I’m building) using this prompt: “Add Tailscale so the pet can reach Hermes from any Wi-Fi, not just my home network. Put it behind an on/off switch in the pet’s settings and keep my local Wi-Fi setup working as before.” I strongly encourage you to try things out like this. And long the way, ask it to explain it to you so you understand the concepts. It’s incredible the things you can do with little to no experience. I’ll be sharing my full AI server setup soon, so follow if you want to see that. #ai #jarvis

Which AI app builder should you use? Lovable vs Bolt vs Replit vs Claude Code If you want to build an app with AI, here's which tool to use, and when to switch. There are two kinds: App builders, where you start. They run in your browser: you describe the app in a chat, it builds it, and it's running a minute later. Hosting and the database are built in. Lovable: the easiest; good-looking apps, fast. Free to try with 5 credits a day; every message uses credits. Bolt: same idea. Describe it, it builds it, it hosts it. Free to start with a monthly allowance. Replit: a full coding workspace under the chat. Free to try, but the free app goes offline after 30 days; the full builder is about $20 a month. Coding agents, for when you get serious. They work on the real code, on your own computer. Claude Code: comes with Claude Pro (about $20 a month). It's what I build with. Codex: OpenAI's version, with ChatGPT. On the $20 plan you get it in the app, your terminal and your code editor. Cursor sits in the middle: a code editor with AI built in. Heads-up: its cheaper plans now only run Grok models; for Claude or GPT you need the $30 plan. The move: start in Lovable, Bolt or Replit. Learn what an app is made of and prove your idea works. Then connect it to GitHub (Lovable and Bolt both let you), and keep building it in Claude Code or Codex. When it's time: when you spend more time fighting the tool than building your app. You don't need to code. But you do need to understand the front end, the back end and the database, how they connect, and how to keep your database secure. How to connect AI to the tools you use at work, inside Claude AI by itself can't do much for your job. It can't see your inbox, your calendar or your clients; it only knows what you paste into the chat. Connect it to your tools, and it has your real context. 1. Connectors. In Claude, open connectors, pick Gmail, Google Calendar, your Drive, your CRM, sign in and approve. Now Claude can search your emails, read your calendar and look up your clients. 2. Your rule book. One file: how you write, who counts as urgent (clients, your boss, anything due this week), what it should never say, how you sign off. Put it in a Claude project and it reads it every time. 3. Give it a job. "Go through my inbox, find everyone who needs an urgent reply, and draft the replies using my rule book." It searches, opens each email, checks your rules, looks at past emails with that person, and writes the drafts. You get a list: who, why it's urgent, and the draft, ready. Every tool it uses shows up in the chat. 4. Permissions. Every tool either reads or writes. By default, Claude asks for your approval before every action it takes for you. You can keep a tool on "always ask", or switch it off. How I'd start: let it read freely, make it ask before it writes, and loosen it one tool at a time once you trust a job. There's an auto mode, but Anthropic says its safety check can miss things, so anything that leaves your company stays on ask. Your inbox is the easiest place to start.
